# AIGC Video Recreation Prompt — Renaissance Collage Edition
## Slot Instructions
ONE replaceable slot: 【Topic】. Ask the user for its content and confirm BEFORE generating; if empty, use the default. No additional slots.
## Module 0 — User Input
**Topic:** 【"Why did Renaissance noblewomen pluck their hairlines? — the 500-year-old 'high forehead' beauty trend"】
**Default:** "Why did Renaissance noblewomen pluck their hairlines? — the 500-year-old 'high forehead' beauty trend"
## Global Specs
- Aspect ratio: 16:9 horizontal
- Hard lock: total = 40.0s, 7 shots, exact integer durations; never exceed
- Language: English only — all on-screen text, quill annotations, labels, subtitles, narration
- Image generation: GPT Image 2.0, 1K resolution (locked)
- Video generation: Seedance 2.0, 720p (locked)
- Narration & music: ElevenLabs; BGM −20 dB vs narration
## Visual Style System (Highest Priority)
Keep the classic explainer SKELETON — collage cut-outs, handwritten annotations, infographic animations — but re-skin EVERY element as authentic European Renaissance art. No modern visual language.
**Skeleton (kept):** cut-out characters/objects WITH consistent clean white die-cut borders (scrapbook collage feel) layered on textured paper backgrounds; handwritten annotations; infographic elements that draw or pop in to explain mechanisms.
**Skin — High Renaissance classical (all shots unless overridden):**
- Cut-outs look scissor-cut from authentic Renaissance oil paintings (manner of Leonardo and Raphael): dignified figures, correct proportions, soft sfumato edges, brushwork and craquelure on the cut-out surface
- Backgrounds: aged parchment / canvas paper texture, warm golden-amber tint; accents of ochre, umber, burnt sienna, crimson, ultramarine — NOT kraft paper
- Soft window / candle light with gentle chiaroscuro on subjects
- Period-accurate 15th–16th century clothing, furniture, props
- Infographic animations = quill-ink drawings animating on parchment (draw / pop in)
**Shot 5 override — Leonardo codex infographic:** sepia ink schematic diagrams on aged parchment, cross-hatching; elements draw themselves like a living notebook.
**Shots 1 & 7 (modern subjects):** modern people/objects as cut-outs STILL painted in the same High Renaissance oil style, as if by Raphael.
**Annotations:** quill-and-ink handwriting only — sepia, aged irregular strokes; arrows, circles, underlines share the texture. No digital fonts or stickers.
**[NEG] negative lock (append to every shot prompt):** No kraft paper, notebook doodle style; no photography, photorealism, anime, flat vector, 3D CGI, watercolor storybook; no non-English or bilingual text; no deformed anatomy, extra limbs, distorted hands, malformed faces, blurry edges, color bleeding; no modern objects in historical scenes; no non-Renaissance rendering on any element.
**Continuity:** all 7 shots share one visual universe — same parchment texture, palette, light. No repeated images.
## Narrative Skeleton
Story FUNCTIONS from the default script. When 【Topic】 changes, keep each shot's function, rhythm, camera language; re-derive subjects; never force default content onto new topics.
| Shot | Function |
|---|---|
| 1 | Modern hook — today's struggle (4s) |
| 2 | The twist — 500 years ago (5s) |
| 3 | The evidence — paintings prove it (6s) |
| 4 | The practice — what they did (6s) |
| 5 | The reason — the mechanism (6s) |
| 6 | The punchline — iconic artwork (6s) |
| 7 | Modern callback + call to action (7s) |
## Shot Breakdown
### Shot 1 — Modern Hook (4s)
- Subject: modern people/products living the daily struggle of 【Topic】, tied to present-day life. *Default:* hair-transplant ad posters, anti-hair-loss shampoo packaging, a crying young person clutching their head
- Camera: rapid flash-cuts between framings, fast montage switching
- Annotations: ironic quill-ink label naming the struggle; ink question marks
- Audio: tense modern BGM; noisy modern ad-clutter SFX
- Prompt: Cut-out figures with white die-cut borders in High Renaissance oil style on aged parchment; the modern-day struggle of 【Topic】 (hair-transplant ads, shampoo packaging, crying balding youth); flash-cut montage; quill-ink label and question marks. [NEG]
### Shot 2 — The Twist (5s)
- Subject: a real famous Renaissance artwork embodying 【Topic】's surprising truth. *Default:* Piero della Francesca's "Portrait of Battista Sforza, Duchess of Urbino" and her high forehead
- Camera: freeze from Shot 1's chaos, then slow push-in on the key detail
- Annotations: quill-ink circle + handwritten question; golden ink shimmer
- Audio: comedic classical orchestral sting
- Prompt: Slow push-in on an authentic Renaissance masterpiece relevant to 【Topic】; quill-ink circle and question on the key detail; golden ink shimmer; faithful to the original. [NEG]
### Shot 3 — The Evidence (6s)
- Subject: 3–4 Renaissance artworks proving 【Topic】's phenomenon was widespread. *Default:* Leonardo and Raphael portraits with high hairlines and missing eyebrows
- Camera: quick cuts between gallery-wall framings
- Annotations: sepia quill-ink circles appear one by one on the recurring detail; one keyword per painting
- Prompt: Gallery montage of authentic Renaissance paintings relevant to 【Topic】; quill-ink circles highlight the recurring detail; warm gallery light; uniform oil texture. [NEG]
### Shot 4 — The Practice (6s)
- Subject: a Renaissance figure performing the ritual behind 【Topic】. *Default:* a noblewoman plucking her hairline with tweezers, wincing
- Camera: medium close-up, slight shake on action
- Annotations: quill-ink SFX words or wry comment
- Audio: playful percussive pops synced to the action
- Prompt: Cut-out figure with white die-cut border in High Renaissance oil style performing the ritual of 【Topic】 on parchment period interior; warm chiaroscuro; comic exaggeration; quill-ink SFX words. [NEG]
### Shot 5 — The Reason (6s)
- Subject: Leonardo codex-style infographic explaining the mechanism (cultural/scientific/historical) of 【Topic】. *Default:* parchment page sketching ideal noble-forehead proportions, plus a banquet vignette of aristocratic status
- Camera: slow pan across the diagram
- Action: elements draw themselves in ink; golden ink highlight on the key factor
- Annotations: 2–4 short handwritten explainer labels
- Audio: curious, scholarly mood
- Prompt: Aged parchment page in Leonardo da Vinci codex style; sepia ink infographic animating to explain 【Topic】's mechanism; handwritten English labels; golden ink highlight; slow pan. [NEG]
### Shot 6 — The Punchline (6s)
- Subject: the most famous artwork tied to 【Topic】 as comedic payoff. *Default:* extreme close-up of the Mona Lisa's browless eyes — "Leonardo didn't forget the eyebrows; that WAS the fashion"
- Camera: dramatic slow zoom; hold a beat with no narration (BGM continues)
- Annotations: one witty quill-ink caption lands the joke
- Audio: playful orchestral punctuation
- Prompt: Extreme close-up on the most iconic artwork related to 【Topic】, faithful to the original; slow zoom on the detail; witty quill-ink caption; warm museum light. [NEG]
### Shot 7 — Modern Callback + CTA (7s)
- Subject: a modern person's humorous, relieved reaction. *Default:* a young person laughing into a mirror, reframed as "Renaissance nobility bloodline"
- Camera: gentle push-in, then pull-back; final 2s fade to black
- Annotations: closing quill-ink call to action (share with a friend)
- Audio: uplifting playful orchestral finale on the laugh
- Prompt: Cut-out figures with white die-cut borders in High Renaissance oil style on aged parchment; modern humorous reaction to 【Topic】's revelation; warm golden light; closing quill-ink call to action; final 2s fade to black. [NEG]
## Audio & Narration (A/V Dual Hard Lock)
- VIDEO TRACK IS INDEPENDENT AND IMMUTABLE: locked at exactly 40.0s. NEVER auto-extend, pad, freeze, or insert still frames to match longer audio. Audio must fit INSIDE the video.
- AUDIO STARTS AT 0.0s: BGM/SFX begin instantly at frame one; narration line 1 within 0.5s. NO silent or muted intro.
- Narration + pauses must END by 38.0s, leaving ≥2s tail for the fade-to-black.
- The FIRST narration line must be a STRONG question fired directly at the viewer — second-person "you", rising incredulous intonation, unmistakable question mark; never a statement. *Default line 1:* "Pills? Transplants? Why does a hairline terrify you?"
- One speaker: young documentary-style English voice, comedic timing, light science storytelling, 145–155 wpm (≈2.5 words/s).
- Script ≤ 80 words total hard cap. Per-shot caps: S1 ≤8, S2 ≤10, S3 ≤12, S4 ≤12, S5 ≤12, S6 ≤12, S7 ≤14 words.
- Pauses: 0.5–0.8s between sentences; never exceed 1.5s.
- Self-check BEFORE TTS: output [Word Count: X] + estimated duration (words ÷ 2.5 + pauses) per shot. If any estimate > shot duration − 0.5s, DELETE WORDS and regenerate, then re-run TTS. NEVER time-stretch, speed up, or pitch-shift audio; NEVER extend the video.
- Clear start and ending. BGM (−20 dB vs narration) arc: S1 tense modern → S2 comedic classical sting → S3–S5 playful classical → S6 comic punctuation → S7 uplifting finale
- SFX: record-scratch at S2 (0.3s accent, NEVER mutes the track); noisy ad clutter in S1; percussive pops in S4; quill scratches on annotations; page-turn / gallery ambience
## Verification (must pass before delivery)
- Narration matches visuals every shot; opening line is a question; A/V synchronized; audio present from 0.0s; TTS ends by 38.0s
- BGM meets −20 dB; total runtime exactly 40.0s; final 2s fade to black; ZERO frozen, padded, or still-substitute frames anywhere
- No repeated images; all on-screen text English only
- Collage + white borders + annotations + infographics intact; every element reads as Renaissance oil / Leonardo manuscript
*New 【Topic】? Supplement visuals per the Visual Style System.*

# Knowledge: Seedance 2.0 Full Production Guide

## Character Consistency

Character identity routing — which reference field to use (images / videos / platform virtual avatars), reuse rules, and reject checks — lives in the `consistency/character-multi-ref` fragment. Load it for any character-consistent Seedance production; it is the single source of truth for identity handling. Seedance-specific reference prep and the hard virtual-avatar rule below still apply.

Fixed-cast stories are character-consistent even when the user does not say "keep them consistent": sports teams, competitions, families, bands, partners, classmates, girl/boy groups, or "N people" who carry the action need character references. Do not write that such people are "only a crowd", "style consistency is enough", or "individual precision is unnecessary" unless they are clearly one-off background extras. For counted fixed casts up to 9 people, list numbered member slots (for example Athlete 1-8) and prepare one reference per member slot; team/crowd collage references are not a substitute for member identity.

**Reference Image Preparation** (critical — do NOT generate separate T2I images for each angle, they will be inconsistent):
1. **Single multi-angle sheet** (preferred): Use `generate_text_to_image` to generate ONE image containing the character from multiple angles (front, side, 3/4 view) in a single picture
2. **I2I derivation**: Generate one initial reference with T2I → use `generate_images_to_image` to derive additional angle variants from that single reference

**⚠️ Platform Virtual Avatars (hard rule — characters marked "Virtual avatar" in their info)**:
- When a referenced character is marked as a virtual avatar (you will see "Virtual avatar" or
  "Also registered as a virtual avatar" in the character info injected with the user message),
  you MUST use `reference_character_ids` with the character's ID — do NOT extract its ref images
  and put them in `reference_image_media_ids`. The harness resolves character IDs to registered
  asset IDs that bypass Seedance's content policy filters. Passing raw ref images directly will
  trigger real-person detection and fail.
- This only applies to `generate_multi_ref_to_video`. For other tools (T2I, I2I, I2V with non-Seedance models) that don't
  support `reference_character_ids`, use the character's ref image IDs normally.

## Scene Consistency

For coherent stories, scene/environment consistency across shots is almost always needed — the same approach as character consistency, but for backgrounds.

**Reference Image Preparation**:
1. **Generate a scene reference**: Use `generate_text_to_image` to create a reference image of the environment/location (e.g. a coffee shop interior, a rainy alley, a spaceship bridge)
2. **Multiple angles** (optional): Generate a single image containing 2–3 views of the same location (wide establishing shot + detail close-up) for stronger environment consistency — same approach as character multi-angle sheets

**Using Scene References**:
- Label scene references with `Scene:` at the top of the prompt (e.g. `Scene: image_6, image_7`)
- The model uses these to maintain consistent background, lighting, and spatial layout across shots
- For multi-shot stories: generate scene references once, reuse across all calls that share the same location
- If the story spans multiple locations, prepare separate scene references for each location
- If the user already uploaded scene/reference images, map each original uploaded media ID to a concrete room/location before planning any shots
- In the final `generate_multi_ref_to_video` call, keep the matching original uploaded media ID in `reference_image_media_ids`; derived images can be added as extra refs, but must not replace the original uploaded image

## Style Consistency (Optional)

When a unified visual style is needed across shots (e.g. a specific art style or color palette), generate a style reference image with `generate_text_to_image`, include it in `reference_image_media_ids`, and label it with `Style:` at the top of the prompt. Describe the style once in the prompt body to reinforce it. Combine with `style_postfix` for best results.

## Audio

- **Audio is always on**: Every Seedance video includes synchronized audio (dialogue, SFX, ambient) by default — there is no separate flag to enable it
- **Use native audio for ALL speech in Seedance workflows (MANDATORY)**: Seedance 2.0 has exceptionally strong native audio — it generates speech with emotion, tone, lip-sync, natural pauses, and breathing. When using the Seedance workflow, you MUST use native audio for ALL speech (dialogue, narration, presentation, voiceover, etc.) instead of TTS. Write speech directly in the video prompt using `says:` syntax. Do NOT use TTS (`generate_text_to_speech`) for Seedance workflows. The ONLY exception is when the user literally says "use TTS" or "use text-to-speech" by name. This rule applies to ALL video types including science explainers, documentaries, tutorials, brand ads, short dramas, and narrated content — write narration as narrator character speech using `says:` syntax
- **"旁白配音" means native narration, NOT TTS**: When a user says "需要旁白配音" or "需要配音", they want spoken narration in the video — they are NOT requesting TTS technology. Implement narration by writing it as a narrator voice in the video prompt using `says:` syntax. For example: `A warm male narrator voice says: "[narration in the task's language]"`. Seedance will generate this narration natively with natural emotion and timing. This IS the "配音" the user wants
- **Why native audio over TTS for Seedance**: Seedance is one of the few models whose native audio quality exceeds TTS — it provides lip-sync, emotional delivery, and natural vocal performance. TTS produces robotic, stiff narration that degrades the quality of story-driven, brand, and emotional content. TTS is only acceptable for pure science/news/tutorial content where a clinical tone is appropriate
- **If TTS is used** (e.g., user explicitly says "use TTS"): generate TTS first, then plan shot timing around the narration duration. Specify "no human speech" in the video prompt so native audio only produces ambient/SFX. **Ensure TTS is not added to shots where the prompt specifies "no human speech" — this constraint must be respected in the final timeline assembly**
- **BGM (Background Music)**: Seedance native audio generates ambient sounds and SFX but does not produce a full background music track. For videos that need BGM, search for a suitable track using `asset_search_bgm`, or generate one with `generate_text_to_music`, then add it to the music track on the timeline
- **Spoken language matching**: All dialogue, narration, voiceover, and spoken content in the video prompt must use the user's explicitly requested spoken language. If no spoken language is specified, use the primary language of the user's task description. Do not translate spoken content into another language unless the user explicitly asks. When the user emphasizes a spoken language preference, include an explicit instruction in the video prompt (e.g. `Spoken language: all dialogue and narration are in English.`)

## Script Writing Conventions

The director_note must contain **complete, ready-to-use prompts** — not outlines or summaries. Default to **medium-to-long narrative complexity**: describe the environment, character micro-actions, emotional beats, and sensory details (see Example 4 below). Only use one-liner prompts for trivially simple scenes (e.g. a single product shot or a quick concept test).

**⚠️ Duration Planning (CRITICAL for videos ≥ 2 minutes)**:
- Seedance 2.0 max clip duration: **15 seconds**
- For a 2-minute video: `ceil(120s / 15s) = 8 clips minimum`
- For a 3-minute video: `ceil(180s / 15s) = 12 clips minimum`
- **Common mistake**: Planning only 4-5 shots for a 2-minute video — this yields ~60-75s max, far below target
- Always calculate: `min_clips = ceil(target_duration / 15)` and ensure your shot list meets this count

When writing the director_note for a Seedance workflow:
- **Reference plan**: List characters/subjects (1 multi-angle sheet per character, or an explicit grouped reference plan for large fixed casts), scenes/locations (1–2 reference images per location), and optionally a style reference. For fixed casts that fit Seedance's image-reference budget (up to 9 people), use one numbered member slot/reference per person instead of crowd or team-collage references, and write the numeric coverage in the plan (for example: "8 athlete references: Athlete 1 ... Athlete 8").
- **Global roster binding**: For fixed casts, write one global `Role → Figure slot → reference variable` map and keep it stable across every clip. Do not reuse a global Figure number for a different character in a later prompt.
- **Prompt drafts**: Write full narrative prompts using the five-element structure (Subject → Action → Camera → Style → Constraints) — include environment atmosphere, character body language, micro-expressions, and audio cues
- **Per-clip reference coverage**: Before each video prompt draft, list which global roster slots appear in the clip and ensure each one has a matching reference in that task. If a named/slotted character appears in the prompt, its reference must be passed to the same `generate_multi_ref_to_video` task.
- **Figure notation**: Use "Figure 1", "Figure 2" to reference characters (never real names). For fixed casts, these are global character slots; if the tool call passes only a subset of references, label the local image with the global slot (for example, `Figure 6 (Rival): image_2`) instead of using only local `image_N` labels or renumbering the character as a different global Figure.
- **Timeline markers**: For multi-shot videos (>5s), use `[00-05s]` markers
- **Audio notes**: Describe desired dialogue/SFX per shot in the prompt
- **Action causality**: For sports, battles, chases, dances, competitions, escapes, or any action-driven story, verify that each clip's result explains the next clip's starting state. If a ball, vehicle, weapon, pursued person, lead performer, or other key object changes position/owner, include the handoff, rebound, block, dodge, pursuit, or reaction that makes the transition believable.

## Workflow
1. Generate ONE multi-angle reference sheet per character/subject (front + side + 3/4 view in a single image)
   - For a counted fixed cast of up to 9 people, each person is a separate character/subject. Generate one reference sheet per member slot (for example Athlete 1, Athlete 2, ... Athlete 8); do not generate a single team, crowd, or group portrait as the identity reference.
2. For coherent stories: generate scene/environment reference images for each location
3. Optionally: generate a style reference image if a specific visual style is needed across shots
4. Optionally add a reference video (motion style) or audio (audio style/mood reference)
5. Write a prompt following the Seedance 2.0 methodology below
6. Call `generate_multi_ref_to_video` with reference media IDs, the prompt, and a `style_postfix` for unified style
   (Mandatory — do not skip this call based on assumptions about service availability. See the Mandatory Execution Attempt rule in the workflow prompt.)
7. When uploaded images are available, the final video call must still include those original uploaded image IDs for the corresponding subject/scene

For fixed-cast character stories, a zero-reference multi-ref call is not a character-consistency route. If identity matters, first obtain character reference media, then pass them through `reference_image_media_ids`, `reference_video_media_ids`, or `reference_character_ids` as appropriate.

If the director_note says references will be generated, those image/reference tasks must be called and waited before the character video call. Do not write a reference plan and then execute the same character shots as "T2V (0 references)".

---

## Seedance 2.0 Prompt Methodology

### Core Principle: Write Intent, Not Details

Seedance 2.0 has built-in director thinking and world knowledge. Do NOT pile up adjectives or micro-manage every frame. The model automatically arranges shots and fills in reasonable details.

Key rules:
1. **Focus on motion** — describe what moves, how fast, and where; skip static appearance when references already define it
2. **Negative prompts don't work** — never write "don't include X"; describe what you want instead
3. **Use specific camera terms** — "slow dolly-in, eye level" works; "dynamic cinematic" is meaningless
4. **Degree adverbs matter** — "swiftly runs" vs "runs" produce very different motion amplitude
5. **One style anchor > many adjectives** — "Wes Anderson palette" beats "pastel, symmetrical, whimsical"

### Five-Element Structure

Follow this order for best results (each element is optional but order matters):

Subject → Action → Camera → Style → (Constraints)

- **Subject** first: locks model attention (use "Figure 1" / "Figure 2" to reference uploaded characters)
- **Action** second: the dynamic anchor — verbs + motion degree
- **Camera** third: shot size + movement + angle (prevents random angle switching)
- **Style** fourth: one visual anchor (film stock, director name, or art movement)
- **Constraints** (optional): guardrails for lighting, color, duration, audio cues — often unnecessary

### Reference Labeling in Prompts

When using multiple reference images for different roles (characters, scenes, props), label them at the top of the prompt so the model knows which image maps to which role:

Figure 1: image_1, image_2, image_3
Figure 2: image_4, image_5
Scene: image_6, image_7

Each label can map to one or more images. Multiple images per label (e.g. different angles of the same character) strengthen identity consistency. Then write the rest of the prompt below. "Figure N" labels character/subject references; "Scene" labels background/environment references. This keeps identity assignment unambiguous when multiple references are passed.

For fixed casts across multiple clips, keep a global roster map outside the local `image_N` array. The `image_N` labels are local to the current tool call; the character alias is global. If Figure 6 is the Rival, every prompt involving that character should label the local reference as `Figure 6 (Rival): image_N`, even when it is local `image_2` in a two-reference clip.

### Multi-Shot (Recommended)

Seedance 2.0 has extremely strong instruction-following for multi-shot. Two approaches:

**Approach 1 — Script-first (preferred, simpler)**:
Write the story directly, then append a multi-shot suffix to let the model design camera work autonomously:

[Story / narrative description here]
Multi-shot, fast cuts, varied shot sizes, includes close-ups and wide shots

The suffix tells the model the desired shot frequency, framing variety, etc. You write the **what** (story); the model decides the **how** (camera angles, cuts, transitions).

**Approach 2 — Full control (detailed)**:
Use **timeline markers** when you want precise control over every shot:

[00-05s] Shot description with specific camera...
[05-10s] Shot description with specific camera...
[10-15s] Shot description with specific camera...

If you specify shots in detail, Seedance follows your design exactly.

**Key difference from Sora / Kling**: Seedance's instruction-following is strong enough that both approaches work reliably — other models may need more explicit shot descriptions to produce good results.

### Duration and Pacing Planning

**Core principle: generate as much story as possible in a single call.** A story that fits in 12s should not be split into two calls — segments generated separately are difficult to keep consistent in voice and style. **Let content determine duration, not the other way around.**

| Content type | Suggested duration |
|-------------|--------------------|
| Single action / product showcase | 4–6s |
| Short emotional scene (no dialogue) | 6–10s |
| Dialogue scene (2–4 lines) | 10–13s |
| Complete short story (multi-character + turn) | 12–15s |

Allow at least 2–3s per dialogue line; when using timeline markers (`[00-05s]`), align them to actual dialogue volume — do not compress 3 lines of dialogue into 4s.

Pacing suffix reference:
- Fast action: `Multi-shot, fast cuts, handheld urgency, wide-to-closeup progression`
- Drama / dialogue: `Multi-shot, medium pacing, shot-reverse-shot during dialogue, close-ups on faces`
- Slow atmosphere: `Single long take` or `Multi-shot, slow pacing, minimal cuts`

### Prompt Examples

Example 1 — One-liner T2V (no references, simplest form)

A golden retriever puppy chases a butterfly across a sunlit meadow, stumbles, rolls over, then bounces back up wagging its tail. Handheld, wide to close-up.

Reference setup: none (pure T2V).

Example 2 — Product showcase (five-element style, compact)

Figure 1: image_1, image_2, image_3

Figure 1 (a minimalist glass perfume bottle). Placed on a white marble surface, water droplets form on the cool glass exterior and slowly trickle down.
Extreme close-up, slow dolly-in, high angle, macro lens.
Studio fashion photography, cool tungsten backlight + soft fill from left, shallow depth of field, muted silver tones.
No text, no hands, no sudden cuts.

Reference setup: 3 product photos (front, side, top).

Example 3 — Script-first multi-shot (no dialogue, model designs camera)

Figure 1: image_1

Figure 1 sprints down the steps of a train station, weaving through commuters. Spots someone waving from the platform — face breaks into a wide grin. Accelerates. The train doors begin to close. Last second, she dives through, collapsing against the doors, breathless, laughing.

Multi-shot, fast cuts, framing progresses from wide establishing to extreme close-up, handheld urgency throughout.

Audio: station ambience, rushing footsteps, crowd murmur, train door chime, relieved exhale.

Reference setup: 1 multi-angle sheet of the character.

Example 4 — Rich narrative multi-shot + dialogue (novelistic detail, model designs camera)

Figure 1: image_1, image_2
Figure 2: image_3, image_4
Scene: image_5

Style: contemporary drama, warm afternoon light filtered through dusty blinds, slice-of-life realism with a Wong Kar-wai melancholy.

The café is almost empty. Afternoon light slants through half-closed venetian blinds, casting striped shadows across the table. A half-finished latte sits untouched, foam long collapsed.

Figure 1 sits alone by the window, one hand wrapped around the cold cup, the other tracing idle circles on the condensation ring it left on the wooden table. Her gaze drifts past the glass — not watching anything, just somewhere far away. A strand of hair falls across her cheek; she doesn't bother to push it back.

The door chime rings. Figure 2 steps in, pauses at the threshold, scanning the room. He spots Figure 1 and something tightens in his jaw — a flicker of hesitation before he walks over, pulling out the chair across from her. The chair leg scrapes against the tile floor.

He sits. A beat of silence. Figure 2 leans forward slightly, elbows on the table, and says in a calm, slightly husky male voice: "You didn't reply to my message."

Figure 1's fingers stop tracing. She looks up — slowly, as if the motion costs her something — meets his eyes for a fraction of a second, then drops her gaze back to the cup. In a quiet, slightly raspy female voice: "I know."

The silence stretches. Somewhere behind the counter, a spoon clinks against ceramic. Figure 2 studies her face, searching. He leans closer.

Figure 2 says softly: "Are you okay?"

Figure 1's composure cracks — just barely. The corner of her mouth twitches upward into a small, sad smile that doesn't reach her eyes. She exhales, almost a laugh, almost a sigh: "I will be."
